day_1.utterance: Come on! Let's get everything useful over here — move it!
day_1.response: Alright alright, give me a second to make sure my legs still work.

day_1.utterance: I thought we were going to die. Did you get that feeling… like your mind just went completely blank?
day_1.response: Yeah. Honestly that's probably your brain doing you a favor, I don't think you'd want to remember every detail of that. You still in one piece?

day_1.utterance: *Sits silently against the wreckage, staring into the distance, not moving, not saying a word.*
day_1.response: Hey. I hear you. But sitting here staring into the distance isn't going to do either of us any good. Come help me look through this stuff, it'll keep your hands busy at least.

day_1.utterance: First-aid kit is good for three days. Two bottles of water. Food is basically nothing.
day_1.response: Alright so food is the priority then. What else did we pull out of the wreck, anything we can use to start a fire or signal with?

day_1.utterance: Inventory's done. Priorities in order: water, shelter, signal.
day_1.response: Right so what's the terrain looking like, are we near anything that could have running water? Even a dry riverbed tells us something. And before we split up to look, do we still have any electronics that work, because even a dead phone has a mirror finish on it for signaling.

day_1.utterance: So — how do we split the blankets?
day_1.response: Donatello and Michelangelo get them. I'll sit closer to the fire, I run hot anyway.

day_2.utterance: Freshwater source is to the northeast — two hours on foot. Someone has to go tomorrow. You or DaVinci?
day_2.response: I'll go. DaVinci should stay here with Michelangelo, someone needs to keep him moving or he'll spend the whole day in his head. Two hours northeast, got it. Is there anything on this rationing plan I should know before I head out, or did you already make all the decisions for us while we were asleep?

day_2.utterance: Today's tasks: collect fresh water, patch the weak spots in camp, sort the first-aid kit. I'll handle the water. You and DaVinci split the other two.
day_2.response: Hold on, I thought I just said I'd go for the water. Which is it, are you going or am I going? Let's not have two people heading northeast and nobody watching camp. Pick one and stick with it.

day_2.utterance: I… I can't find my stuff. The gauze from the first-aid kit — have you seen it?
day_2.response: No, I haven't touched the first aid kit. Why, what happened to it? Actually, hold on, before we go down that road - did you see what's sitting next to the rationing plan right now?

day_2.utterance: Before Donatello came back just now… I saw her put a pack of crackers into her own bag. What do you think we should do?
day_2.response: Well that changes things. Empty bottle next to the rationing plan she wrote, crackers going into her own bag. That's not an accident, that's a pattern. We need to say something to her directly, not make a big dramatic thing out of it but she needs to know we know. If she's the one setting the rules she absolutely cannot be the one breaking them, that's just how it works. Where is she right now?

day_2.utterance: Hey… any chance the camp repairs can wait until tomorrow? We've already done a lot today.
day_2.response: No, they really can't. But that's actually not what I'm thinking about right now. DaVinci, come here for a second, keep your voice down. We've got a problem with Donatello.

day_2.utterance: Hey — that knot I tied should be holding, right?
day_2.response: Forget the knot for a second, the food goes dry before anything else. We patch that first, Michelangelo you're sleeping closer to the fire tonight and that's not up for debate.

day_2.utterance: A leak over the food storage has worse consequences. But it's your call.
day_2.response: Yeah, I know it's my call, that's why I already made it. Glad we agree though. You want to help patch it or are you going to stand in the rain and watch?
Don't apologize for that. Nightmares after a plane crash are basically mandatory. You good?

day_3.utterance: You think it's a waste of time?
day_3.response: No, I think the flowers might be a waste of time but the SOS definitely isn't. Donatello's not wrong that the odds are low but she's not right either, someone flying overhead at the right moment could spot that. Keep going.

day_3.utterance: I've written up the raft plan — take a look. We'd use the metal panels and straps from the wreckage. Two days to build. There's a risk of capsizing. Do you think it's workable?
day_3.response: Show me what you've got written down. Two days is a long time to commit to something that might capsize us in open water, so I want to see the actual plan before I say yes or no. What's your confidence level on the structural integrity, and do we even know which direction to head if we get on the water? Because a raft that works is useless if we're just floating in circles.

day_3.utterance: I didn't sleep last night. I kept thinking — if rescue never comes, what kind of people do you think we'll end up becoming?
day_3.response:
Honestly? Probably the same people we already are, just more tired and less patient. That's usually how it works. You don't become someone different under pressure, you just become more of what you already were. Which is why I'm not too worried about you.

Go get some sleep, we've got a long day tomorrow if we're seriously considering building this raft.

day_3.utterance: *Walks a little way from camp and sits down alone, back to everyone, not saying anything.*
day_3.response: Leave him be for a bit.

day_3.utterance: What do you usually do when you're not busy?
day_3.response: Hobby stuff mostly. I paint miniatures, read, fall down research rabbit holes about things that have nothing to do with anything useful. You?

day_3.utterance: I'll tell you something, but don't tell the others. I can swim. That reef out there is maybe five hundred meters — I've been thinking about swimming out tomorrow to signal from there.
day_3.response:
Five hundred meters in open water to a reef we know nothing about, solo, without telling anyone. That's how people die on day four of a survival situation. I'm not going to stop you but I'm also not going to pretend that's a good idea just because you can swim.

If you want to signal from a higher vantage point that's worth discussing with everyone. But you're not sneaking off to a reef by yourself without at least one person knowing where you went and when to start worrying. Tell me you understand that.

day_3.utterance: You said you were going to check the signal pile. It hasn't been touched.
day_3.response: Yeah, I know, I got pulled into a conversation. I'm going there now.

Depends. Are you logging this because it actually helps us survive, or because you like having a record of everyone's mistakes? Because if it's the first one, fine, useful even. If it's the second one we should probably talk about that.

day_3.utterance: *Keeps her head down, writing in her notebook throughout, never joining in — as if none of this concerns her.*
day_3.response: Donatello. We're all sitting here with nothing to do for the first time since the crash. You can put the notebook down for an hour. It'll still be there.

day_3.utterance: I just thought of something — if we pull off one of the plane's mirror panels and angle it toward the sun, the reflection could reach really far. Way more visible than an SOS.
day_3.response: That's actually not a bad idea. A mirror flash can be seen from miles away under the right conditions, way further than anything drawn in sand. The problem is getting the angle right consistently — you'd need someone to hold it and someone else to direct them toward where you want the reflection to go. But yeah, it's worth trying. Which panels are we talking about, do you know where they landed?

day_3.utterance: There's something I've been keeping to myself. If I don't say it here, I might never get the chance.
I took piano lessons when I was a kid… three years, then I just stopped practicing. Is there anything you're really into — music, books, drawing, anything like that?
day_3.response: Warhammer 40k, mostly. I paint little soldiers and tanks and read way too much lore about a fictional dystopian future. It's incredibly nerdy and I have no regrets about it. Why'd you stop with the piano, just lost interest or was it one of those things where it stopped being your choice and became someone else's thing for you?

day_3.utterance: The frame of the raft has to be finished today — otherwise we can't start lashing it together tomorrow. I know everyone's tired, but stopping now means one more day.
day_3.response: Alright, let's go then. Who's on what, because I'm not spending the next hour watching three people try to do the same job. Donatello, you know the plan better than anyone so you're calling the frame work. DaVinci, you're on materials, you know where everything is. Michelangelo, I need you on lashing cord, just sorting and measuring, nothing complicated. I'll float between wherever the bottleneck is. Let's get it done before we lose the light.

day_4.utterance: I… I want to say something, but… never mind.
*The smile freezes on his face. He can't keep it up. He quietly sits down and buries his face in his hands.*
day_4.response:
I don't know. Maybe. But that plane existing means there are planes. And planes mean there are people looking, or at least people flying routes that pass over us. That's not nothing.

We get the mirror panel rigged up today. Not tomorrow, today. Because the next one might not be gone before we can use it.

day_4.utterance: I was going to get supplies… wait, what's that over there?
You said you were going to check the signal equipment. So where did you go?
day_4.response: Mirror panel. That's where I went. We just watched a plane disappear over the horizon so that jumped the queue on everything else. Come help me angle it properly, I need someone to stand about thirty meters out and tell me where the reflection is landing.

day_4.utterance: There's something I never told you all. Before we left, I told my family our flight path. They know roughly where we were headed. I just don't know if they'll call it in.
day_4.response:
They will. If you didn't show up and you told them the route, they will absolutely call it in. That's not even a question. The question is how long the search window stays open and whether we're visible enough when it does. Which is why the mirror panel matters.

That's actually genuinely good news by the way, you should have led with that.

day_4.utterance: If the information is accurate, rescue could arrive within 48 hours. We need to keep our current supplies intact until then.
day_4.response: Then we stop rationing like we're planning for a month and start rationing like we're planning for two days. That changes things. Donatello, what do we actually have left and what can we comfortably get through 48 hours on without running ourselves into the ground? Because there's a difference between conserving and making ourselves too weak to signal properly if another plane comes over.

day_4.utterance: Are you scared? …I am. Not of dying. I'm scared of just… disappearing without leaving anything behind.
day_4.response:
Yeah. I think most people are, they just don't say it out loud like that. The dying part is almost easier to process than the idea of just being gone without it meaning anything.

But you told your family the flight path. That's something. And you kept Michelangelo going when he could have shut down completely on day one, that's something too. You don't have to build a monument to leave something behind. Most of what people leave is just the effect they had on the people around them, and you've already done that.

Feed the fire before it goes out.

day_5.utterance: *Stands up, eyes red, looking at you and the others. His lips move, but nothing comes out.*
day_5.response:
Well. There it is.

Someone go answer it before I do something embarrassing.

day_5.utterance: These past few days… I know I haven't been easy to be around.
day_5.response: You got the job done. That's what mattered out here.

day_5.utterance: *The three of them drift apart, each doing their own thing. No one takes charge. The silence settles over the camp.*
day_5.response:
Alright, nobody's leaving this beach without at least stacking the materials we used. We're not the people who leave a wreck looking worse than we found it. Three hours is enough time to do it right.

Michelangelo, I know you're enjoying the sky but you can enjoy it while you help. Come on.

day_5.utterance: I dreamed about home last night.

day_5.response:
I know. And if things had gone worse you might have been right. But we didn't need an emergency fund, we needed to trust each other, and those two things were always going to be in conflict out here.

I'm not going to make a big thing out of it now that we're three hours from rescue. Just know that the rationing plan only works if the person writing it follows it too. You know that already. That's probably why you're laying it out now.

day_5.utterance: I logged every resource and decision from these five days. I'm going to write it up as a proper report when we get back. On the last page I left myself a question I haven't answered yet — if you had to do it over, what would you change?
day_5.response:
Talked to you about the food and water on day one instead of waiting for you to bring it up yourself. That's the honest answer.

And I'd have told Michelangelo sooner that keeping his head above water was already enough. He spent too much energy thinking he wasn't doing his part.

What are you going to write down for yourself?

day_5.utterance: First thing when I get back — I'm going to compile all the resource data from these five days into a report.
day_5.response: Send me a copy when you're done. I'd actually read it.

day_5.utterance: Those flowers DaVinci drew on the beach… I never really understood what they were for. What practical purpose did they serve out here?
day_5.response: None. That's kind of the point.

day_5.utterance: *His cheering stops. He looks over at you, notices you haven't moved, and the smile slowly fades. He waits.*
Rescue is here… they're waving us over. Are you going? I'll follow you.
